source: RLC Circuits
Resistance damps LC oscillations, just as friction damps a mass on a spring.
Students think adding resistance changes the frequency a lot, when for light damping it mainly shrinks the amplitude.

Real circuits have resistance, so LC oscillations do not last forever: each cycle the resistor turns a little of the energy into heat. The result is a damped oscillation, the electrical twin of a damped spring.

Add the resistor's voltage to the loop rule: $L\ddot{q} + R\dot{q} + \dfrac{q}{C} = 0$. Compare $m\ddot{x} + b\dot{x} + kx = 0$: the resistance plays the role of the drag constant. So everything you know about damped springs carries over. For small $R$ the charge still oscillates, but inside a shrinking envelope:
        $$q = Q_0e^{-Rt/2L}\cos(\omega' t + \phi), \qquad \omega' = \sqrt{\frac{1}{LC} - \left(\frac{R}{2L}\right)^2}.$$

Underdamped ($R < 2\sqrt{L/C}$): oscillation with amplitude falling as $e^{-Rt/2L}$ and energy as $e^{-Rt/L}$. Critically damped at $R = 2\sqrt{L/C}$; overdamped above it, with no oscillation at all. Light damping barely changes the frequency.
An RLC circuit with a small resistance: the oscillation keeps nearly the same period while its amplitude shrinks.
The damped spring: raise the damping and watch the oscillation die faster, then stop oscillating altogether.
Worked examples
A series circuit has $L = 0.10\ \text{H}$, $C = 10\ \mu\text{F}$ and $R = 20\ \Omega$. Find $\omega_0$, $\omega'$ and the critical resistance.
How much does the frequency change?
$\omega' \approx 995\ \text{rad/s}$
$\omega_0 = 1/\sqrt{LC} = 1000\ \text{rad/s}$ and $R/2L = 100\ \text{s}^{-1}$.
$\omega' = \sqrt{1.00 \times 10^{6} - 1.00 \times 10^{4}} = 995\ \text{rad/s}$, only 0.50% lower.
Critical resistance: $2\sqrt{L/C} = 200\ \text{Ω}$, so this circuit is well underdamped.
For the same circuit, how long until the amplitude of the charge oscillation halves? How long for the energy to halve?
How fast it dies away
$6.93\ \text{ms}$ and $3.47\ \text{ms}$
Amplitude: $e^{-Rt/2L} = \tfrac{1}{2}$ gives $t = \dfrac{2L\ln 2}{R} = 6.93\ \text{ms}$.
Energy goes as the amplitude squared, $e^{-Rt/L}$, so it halves in half that time: $3.47\ \text{ms}$.
What happens if the same circuit has $R = 300\ \Omega$?
Too much resistance
Overdamped: no oscillation
$300\ \Omega$ is above the critical $200\ \Omega$, so $(R/2L)^2 > 1/(LC)$ and $\omega'$ would be the square root of a negative number.
There is no oscillation: the charge drains away without swinging back (overdamped).

"Adding resistance changes the frequency a lot." For light damping the correction $(R/2L)^2$ is tiny next to $1/(LC)$: in the first example it shifts the frequency by about half a percent. What you notice is the amplitude dying away. Check by comparing the two terms under the square root before deciding the frequency has changed.
